title: 18 Trucks at HYBE, 513K Signatures, and a BTS Producer Swearing at Fans — Inside the ENGENE Meltdown
excerpt: Three days after Heeseung left ENHYPEN, 18 protest trucks lined up outside HYBE headquarters. Over 513,000 fans signed a petition in 24 hours. Then a BTS producer used profanity to tell fans to back off. Here's the full story of how K-pop's latest fan uprising got completely out of hand.
author: MEARROW Editorial Desk
content:
On March 10, BELIFT LAB announced that Heeseung would be leaving ENHYPEN.

By March 11, 18 protest trucks were parked outside HYBE's headquarters in Seoul.

By March 12, a BTS producer had used explicit profanity in a public message aimed at ENHYPEN fans.

In under 72 hours, what began as a K-pop group restructuring announcement became one of the most chaotic fan uprisings in recent K-pop history. Here is everything that happened — and why it went this far.

## The Setup: Why ENGENE Didn't Accept This Quietly

When BELIFT LAB announced Heeseung's departure, they framed it as a mutual decision. But a single line in Heeseung's own farewell letter on Weverse changed the entire conversation:

**"I decided to follow the direction suggested by the company."**

That phrase — "the direction suggested by the company" — is not how voluntary departures are typically worded in K-pop. Fans know the difference between "I wanted this" and "the company proposed this and I accepted." The ambiguity was immediate, and ENGENE's reaction was accordingly immediate.

[Related: Was Heeseung Pushed Out? ENHYPEN's Shocking 6-Member Announcement](/en/news/enhypen-heeseung-departure-belift-lab-controversy-2026)

## The Trucks

K-pop fans have used protest trucks outside entertainment company headquarters for years. It began as a fringe tactic and became mainstream during the Goo Hara and Sulli controversies, later deployed by fans of EXO, 2PM, and most recently NewJeans. The trucks carry LED screens with messages — sometimes demands, sometimes tributes — and park in public view for paid, time-limited slots.

By March 11, international ENGENE had funded and deployed **18 trucks** outside HYBE's building simultaneously. The messages called for Heeseung's reinstatement to ENHYPEN and demanded BELIFT LAB provide a transparent explanation for why concurrent solo and group activity was deemed impossible. By some accounts, the display was the largest coordinated truck protest in K-pop history by a single fandom in response to a single event.

HYBE staff arriving for work were photographed reading the messages. According to fan accounts on the ground, employees were observed discussing the displays as they entered the building. No official response from HYBE or BELIFT LAB was issued.

## 513,000 Signatures in 24 Hours

While the trucks gathered outside, international fans launched a Change.org petition titled "Allow Heeseung to Pursue Solo and Group Activities Simultaneously." Within 24 hours of the departure announcement, the petition had collected over **513,000 signatures** — a number that reflects the scale of ENHYPEN's international fandom, which skews heavily toward Southeast Asia, North America, and Latin America.

The core argument: BTS members had maintained solo careers alongside group activities for years. SHINee, EXO, GOT7 — simultaneous solo and group work is standard in K-pop. The petition demanded BELIFT LAB explain specifically why Heeseung could not do the same.

BELIFT LAB did not respond to the petition.

## When Fans Went Too Far

Alongside the organized protests came behavior that drew criticism from outside ENGENE — and from some within it.

Fans began flooding the comment sections of unrelated K-pop artists' social media accounts with demands about Heeseung. BTS members' posts, BLACKPINK's accounts, and several smaller artists found themselves buried under off-topic comments from ENGENE demanding HYBE take action. The logic — that spamming connected artists would pressure HYBE — made sense as a theory but generated significant backlash in K-pop communities.

Korean netizens, in particular, were unimpressed. The consensus on Korean platforms including TheQoo and Nate Pann was consistent: Heeseung himself said it was his decision. Pressuring the company through other artists' pages achieves nothing and embarrasses the fan community.

![18 protest trucks lined up outside HYBE headquarters in Seoul with LED displays calling for Heeseung's return to ENHYPEN](/images/news/enhypen-heeseung-protest-trucks-el-capitxn-2026-thumbnail.webp)
_Image: AI-generated via ChatGPT_

## EL CAPITXN: The BTS Producer Who Snapped

Then came the incident that made the story international.

EL CAPITXN is a producer known for his work with BTS — credits that include collaborations with members during their solo careers. He is also publicly known to have a personal friendship with Heeseung. When Heeseung's departure was announced, ENGENE fans began directing messages at EL CAPITXN, with some accusing him of influencing Heeseung's decision to leave the group.

On March 12, EL CAPITXN posted a response on social media that was unambiguous in its frustration.

"Stop sending me messages about Heeseung. This is getting ridiculous. If you're actually his fan, support him. Why are you blaming me?"

When a fan replied, "Without Lee Heeseung, there would be no fans," EL CAPITXN's response escalated further — using explicit language to tell fans to stop contacting him. He later closed comments on the post. According to reporting by Sportskeeda and allkpop, the phrase "go play on Twitter" featured prominently in a follow-up message he posted before deleting.

The backlash to EL CAPITXN's posts was split. International ENGENE were furious. K-pop observers outside the fandom largely sided with the producer. The broad internet reaction was captured in a Sportskeeda headline that got widely shared: **"This is getting embarrassing."**

## HYBE Staff's Reaction to the Trucks

Fan accounts from the protest scene at HYBE noted something unexpected: HYBE employees who encountered the trucks as they arrived for work were not hostile. Some were observed reading the messages carefully. A few were reported to have briefly acknowledged protesters. None spoke on the record.

Whether this amounts to anything substantive is unknowable. HYBE issued no statement. But the image of staff pausing outside their own building to read LED displays demanding an artist's return is not a flattering one for a company already under significant scrutiny from K-pop fans globally.

## ENHYPEN's First Appearance as Six

On March 12 — the same day EL CAPITXN's posts went viral — three ENHYPEN members (Jay, Jungwon, and Sunghoon) appeared publicly at a Prada event in Seoul. It was the group's first public appearance since the departure announcement.

The optics were difficult. Standing as three rather than seven, at a fashion event rather than a music stage, two days after one of their most viral controversies — the images circulated online and generated their own wave of emotional fan content. Video of Sunoo on a fan call, visibly emotional, spread widely.

The remaining six members posted a joint message to fans stating they would "grow even more from now on" and promising to "deliver even more energetic performances." For many fans, it read less as reassurance and more as confirmation that the transition is real and the number is now fixed.

## The Fault Line: International vs. Korean Fandom

This story has exposed a recurring divide in K-pop fan communities.

International ENGENE, particularly from non-Korean-speaking markets, have pushed hard for Heeseung's return, funded the trucks, organized the petition, and flooded social media. The framing is activist: companies should be held accountable, fans can force change, and public pressure is a legitimate tool.

Korean ENGENE and broader Korean K-pop communities have largely rejected this framing. The position most commonly stated on Korean platforms: Heeseung said it himself. He made a choice. Continuing to pressure the company is not respecting the artist — it's overriding his stated decision. Several Korean fans pointed out that organizing trucks and petitions over an artist's voluntary career change treats Heeseung as property rather than as a person.

Both positions have internal logic. Neither has moved the company.

## MEARROW's Take

Three things stand out from this week's ENGENE situation.

**First, the ambiguity created by BELIFT LAB's communication was entirely avoidable.** If Heeseung's departure was genuinely voluntary, a transparent explanation of why simultaneous solo-group activity was not viable would have closed most questions. The company chose not to provide one. Fan speculation fills the silence.

**Second, fandom protest infrastructure has outpaced fandom judgment.** Eighteen trucks in 24 hours represents real logistical coordination and real money spent — reportedly tens of thousands of dollars combined. That infrastructure now deploys faster than fans can evaluate whether deploying it is appropriate. The truck protest as a tool was designed for genuine artist welfare concerns — blacklisting, contract abuse, unsafe working conditions. Applying it to a career trajectory decision makes the tool itself less credible.

**Third, EL CAPITXN's reaction was understandable but counterproductive.** A personal friend of Heeseung posting aggressively in public during the peak of the controversy fed the story rather than containing it. His frustration is visible and probably warranted. But the posts guaranteed another news cycle.

The central question — whether Heeseung's departure was his own choice or a HYBE-directed decision — remains unanswered. BELIFT LAB's silence on the specific issue of why concurrent activity was impossible means fans have nothing to anchor onto except that one phrase in his farewell letter.

"The direction suggested by the company."

Until that's addressed, the trucks aren't the last thing that will park outside HYBE.
